https://www.dw.com/en/why-are-european-b.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MMvF In an age of geopolitical unrest, more and more countries want to have easy access to their gold reserves Image: CFOTO/picture alliance Advertisement Fort Knox, the fortified complex in the state of Kentucky where around half of the US government's gold reserves are held, is a byword for security. To be "like Fort Knox" means to be extremely secure and well-guarded. Yet the perception of the US as a whole as a secure location to store gold is clearly on the wane. The decision by the Dutch central bank recently to move some 86 tonnes (95 US tons) of gold from New York to London highlighted growing concerns among some governments over storing strategic assets in the US and whether they could be readily accessed in a crisis. The De Nederlandsche Bank (DNB) cited "geopolitical unrest" and said moving its gold across different jurisdictions would improve its "crisis preparedness". France also removed all its remaining gold exposure from the New York Federal Reserve between July 2025 and January 2026, although the Bank of France governor François Villeroy de Galhau said at the time it was not politically motivated. The Dutch have moved their gold to the Bank of England Image: Peter Nicholls/REUTERS Several politicians in Germany and Italy — which hold the world's second- and third-largest gold reserves respectively — have called for their countries' gold to be also taken out of the US amid concerns over the Trump administration's unpredictable policymaking and its growing antipathy towards the EU, including threats to annex part of its territory in Greenland. The gold rush Sebastien Tillett, an analyst with Oxford Economics, says that for European central banks, outright seizure of their assets is an "extremely remote risk". However, he says there are growing concerns over ease of access in an age of geopolitical uncertainty. "The more relevant concern is that assets held in another jurisdiction could become temporarily inaccessible in an extreme sanctions, legal or geopolitical scenario," he told DW. Krishnan Gopaul from the World Gold Council says that in general, central banks around the world have been buying more gold since the 2008 global financial crisis and are increasingly focused on where and how they store it. As a result, gold prices have soared to record highs. A recent survey by the World Gold Council found that central banks have accumulated an average of 1,000 tonnes of gold over the past four years, up from the 500-ton average over the preceding decade. Gopaul says that because the 2008 global financial crisis was followed by the euro sovereign debt crisis and then a variety of political crises, a pandemic, and sustained geopolitical upheaval and conflict, gold has come into sharper focus as a safe haven asset. "As we've gone through the last two decades, there have been questions and concerns around the global financial system and the state of geopolitics in one form or another," he says. The decisions by the Dutch and French to move their gold out of the US and back to Europe highlight the new focus on where exactly the gold is held, so that it can be easily and quickly leveraged in the event of a new crisis. Central banks, governments and sovereign wealth funds hold physical gold in different locations. Moving it can be extremely complex, risky and costly, while the ease of selling it or trading it for currencies or other assets depends on the location. "Central banks are paying greater attention to where reserves are held as well as what assets they hold, mainly to maximise resilience and flexibility of reserve holdings," says Tillett. Gopaul says reserve management has become "incredibly important" and that while it might seem obvious to focus on the possible negative risks associated with a certain jurisdiction such as the US, part of the rationale behind such decisions is making sure the gold is as close to home as possible and in a trading hub which moves fast. He highlights the fact that the Dutch central bank moved its gold to London rather than to the Netherlands because the UK is "one of the most liquid trading hubs in the gold market." "The idea is that in the event of a crisis, in stress periods, that gold can be potentially mobilized," he says. "London is pretty much the heart of the gold market, and there is so much activity there, and it's such a liquid market, that in a time of crisis that is where you want your gold." The Bank of England is a major global gold holder and custodian. There are estimated to be around 400,000 gold bars in its possession, worth around $270 billion (€232 billion). The US question While moving gold to a location such as London has an attraction of its own for European entities, it is clear that doubts over US reliability in the Trump era and over the US financial system as a whole is driving decision-making. Last week, the manager of Norway's massive $2.3 trillion sovereign wealth fund said the fund needs to significantly cut its exposure to US treasuries. That decision seems to be driven by concern over US government bond markets, with soaring inflation and government debt driving up borrowing costs and spooking investors. Tillett says gold remains sensitive to decisions by the US federal reserve and that general concern over US financial markets means gold holders are looking to move their assets. As well as those specific financial market concerns, Trump's rhetoric around Greenland and continued veiled threats towards the EU has added to the reasons for European institutions to want to move their assets around. US President Trump's threats against Greenland alarmed EU leaders Image: Federico Parra/Odd Andersen/AFP Yet the US, and the New York Federal Reserve in Manhattan in particular, remains a key custodian of much European gold, not least from Germany. Although the Bundesbank moved around 300 tonnes of gold back to Germany from the US between 2013 and 2017 , it still holds well over 1,000 tonnes in the US. Last year in a statement it said: "We have no doubt that the New York Fed is a trustworthy and reliable partner for the safekeeping of our gold reserves." Announcements Click here to receive this news directly in your inbox Download Our App Job Board → See More Supply Chain & Operations Coordinator Strategic Account Executive Head Grower – Commercial Tomato Greenhouse Country Director Vietnam Breeding Assistant Grower Funny Looks like I’ll be sleeping on the sofa again tonight In January, farmers across Europe watched the negotiations on the EU-Mercosur trade agreement with suspicion. "Unfair competition," was their verdict. Opening the doors would give a disproportionate advantage to produce grown at lower cost and under less strict labour, health and environmental standards, at the expense of European production. Although it initially looked as though the agreement would be put on ice — the European Parliament asked the Court of Justice of the EU for its opinion on the legal basis — the European Commission, following ratification by Argentina, Uruguay, Brazil and Paraguay, began the provisional application of the agreement. The use of crop protection products that are banned in the EU is one of the sore points in this story. It is a widely shared concern among growers, not only in view of free trade agreements but with regard to all fruit and vegetable imports from third countries. But what do the figures actually say? We dug into the tables to find out where, how often, and which maximum residue levels — the so-called MRLs — were exceeded last year. These violations indicate how much the "level playing field" on crop protection is lacking. It is a fact that in third countries, depending on the country, certain pesticides, fungicides and herbicides — so-called crop protection products, or perhaps more accurately, pest control products — are permitted where they are not in the EU. Turkish growers, for instance, may still apply phosmet, an insecticide, to their crops until at least 2033, while approval for use on European fields expired in 2022. But even within the EU itself, there is no "level playing field". A French grower, for example, may use certain herbicides containing the active substance halosulfuron-methyl, while this is prohibited in the Netherlands. In the Netherlands, in turn, a fungicide containing flutianil is permitted, which is not the case in Spain. Before we look at the residue limit exceedances, this brings us to the question of which various European and national authorities have a hand in policy and enforcement. EFSA, RASFF, NVWA and Ctgb EFSA (European Food Safety Authority) assesses microbiological hazards (such as Salmonella and Listeria), contaminants, additives, GMOs and crop protection products. It provides scientific advice as a basis for EU legislation. RASFF (Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed) is the European warning system for risks in food, feed and food contact materials. All EU member states plus Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein and Switzerland participate. Its purpose is rapid information exchange, so that countries can act in a coordinated way without losing time. When crop protection product limits on fruit and vegetables are exceeded, this can lead to extra checks, blocking, recall or destruction/return of the goods. However, RASFF does not carry out inspections itself, does not impose fines and does not take legal decisions; that remains a task for national authorities. In the Netherlands, for instance, the NVWA is the competent authority for supervision and enforcement of food and feed safety. The NVWA carries out checks at border control posts and within the market through risk-based inspections of growers, importers, retailers and the hospitality sector. If it identifies a serious, potentially cross-border risk, it files a RASFF notification. Notifications from other countries that affect the Netherlands are investigated and handled nationally by the NVWA. Not every national incident ends up in RASFF. The NVWA carries out checks and enforcement on the basis of EU legislation and the decisions of the Ctgb, which in the Netherlands is responsible for authorising crop protection products and biocides. Even where a product has EU approval, the Ctgb can decide, because of specific Dutch circumstances, not to permit its use in the Netherlands. In this way, each EU country has a body responsible for setting the rules and a body that carries out the checks. Emergency exemptions In other words: pesticides banned by the EU are excluded from use in every EU country, but on top of that, each member state can decide on an even stricter policy. Even so, member states can be granted an exemption in the event of an emergency, allowing non-authorised crop protection products to be used temporarily. This exemption system, too, can give rise to discontent among growers. In early March, Sara Rubira, regional minister of Agriculture for the Murcia region, noted that other European countries — such as Portugal, Italy, Greece, Germany, Slovenia and France — have already granted exceptional authorisation to certain products that are still banned in open-field cultivation in Spain. "That creates an unequal playing field and a loss of competitiveness for Spanish growers," she stressed. EU Pesticides Database The limits for crop protection product residues on fruit and vegetables are set at EU level and apply to every member state. They can be found in the EU Pesticides Database. In principle, individual countries cannot set their own standards here. For substances that are banned in European cultivation but permitted in some third countries in the field or greenhouse, MRLs also apply on import, usually a default value: the detection limit for that specific substance, which usually coincides with the standard value of 0.01 mg/kg. In most cases, this means that the substance may not be used in third countries on food destined for export to the EU. But because not every consignment of fruit and vegetables is checked for MRLs — more on that later — this does not always stop growers in third countries from applying these active substances to their crops. It is even the case that certain chemical products banned in European cultivation are produced in Europe and subsequently exported to third countries. Role and risks of crop protection products Setting limits for residues has a clear rationale: the use of pest control products can have adverse effects on the environment and non-target organisms, often without this being immediately visible. Ecosystems can be affected, bee colonies can disappear, and soil, food, groundwater and drinking water can become contaminated. In humans, intake through inhalation, skin contact or food can, depending on the amount, intensity and frequency, potentially lead to serious and chronic conditions such as fertility problems, tumours, neurodegenerative diseases and DNA damage. Conclusively linking health problems to a specific active substance is not easy, not least because the effects usually do not appear in the short term. Moreover, risk assessment is based on laboratory tests of one particular active substance at a time. Research into the effects of exposure to a cocktail of substances — which in practice is more often the case than not — is scarce. Intake through the mouth can be partly avoided by washing fruit and vegetables thoroughly before consumption. However, a thorough wash often does not remove all substances. So peel them, then. Yet part of the active substances is not on the peel but in the flesh itself, absorbed during growth through the sap flow. If you want no — or as little as possible — pesticide residue in your body, organic is the best choice. Of course, there are also advantages that offset the disadvantages, and these are precisely the reason crop protection products are used: they lead to higher yields, more uniform produce and less need for labour and energy in cultivation. And here we touch on the area of food security (at macro level) and income security (at micro level). Of course, the question can be raised whether these benefits could not be achieved in another, safer way. The use of crop protection products ultimately carries certain societal costs, including bee mortality, soil pollution, and costs for drinking water purification and healthcare. Efforts are certainly being made in this regard. Breeding is part of the answer, alongside integrated pest management and other innovative, often technological tools, of which UVC light — which can destroy the DNA of viruses, bacteria and fungi — can serve as an example. This article does not go into the question of alternatives to crop protection products, nor does it address individual product authorisations or the level of MRLs. Interceptions Maximum residue levels are set by the European Commission on the recommendation of EFSA for the sake of food safety. However, crop protection product residues are not the only hazards in this respect. Interceptions of consignments of fruit or vegetables at the EU's external borders can also result from physical hazards (presence of glass, plastic, wood, metal, etc.), microbiological hazards (presence of harmful bacteria, fungi, viruses or parasites) and other chemical hazards (mycotoxins, heavy metals, allergens, etc.), as well as problems with documents or certificates. Of the 5,329 food-related notifications on the RASFF platform in 2025, 1,053 concerned vegetables, fruit and dried fruit (20%). Nuts are not included. They form a separate category and account for 411 cases (8%), the majority of which (86%) is attributable to mycotoxins, mainly aflatoxin. Mycotoxins are toxic substances resulting from mould growth during the storage of, among other things, grain, nuts and coffee under warm and humid conditions. Mould toxins In RASFF's nut statistics, EU countries are responsible for 5% of the alerts. The remaining 95% comes from third countries. Of that, 24% is attributable to the US. Next come Argentina, Turkey, Iran, Georgia, India, China and Egypt. This does not mean, however, that the US or Argentina are less careful with mycotoxins than other suppliers. If we compare these percentages with each country's share in the export of nuts from third countries to the EU, we see that the US, Argentina and China generate fewer notifications than their weight in exports would suggest. The opposite is true for the other countries mentioned above, which give rise to more notifications than their market share would lead one to expect. Chile deserves a special mention: although it accounts for almost 7% of nut supply to the EU, it was not caught out on mycotoxins even once last year. © FreshPlaza Not entirely unexpectedly, half of the violations were recorded by the import and transit country, the Netherlands. Italy, a major producer of nut-based derivative products, accounted for 15%. Germany, the largest EU market, reported 11% of cases, and Bulgaria, the border country through which most nuts from Turkey, Georgia, Azerbaijan and Iran enter the EU, filed 7% of the alerts in the RASFF system. MRLs in intra-European trade Document problems, physical and microbiological hazards, and finally heavy metals and allergens together accounted for 242 notifications in the RASFF system for fruit and vegetables. That is 23%. This brings us to the calculation that just over half (577 cases, or 55%) were for exceedances of crop protection product residue limits. Of these, 15% were attributable to violations by European companies, while 85% were identified in imports from third countries. © FreshPlaza In intra-European trade, Italy and Spain, major cross-border fruit and vegetable suppliers, each account for a quarter of the alerts. Poland, Belgium, Greece and the Netherlands each hover around 10%. France, Bulgaria, Denmark, Hungary and Latvia also appear in the statistics, with percentages between 1% and 3%. A fifth of notifications concern exceedances of MRLs for products banned in the EU, with the insecticide chlorpyrifos, banned since 2020, standing out as an outlier (more than half of these cases). Poland complied least with the rules on banned products (33%), followed by Spain (22%). © FreshPlaza In intra-European trade, most limit exceedances were recorded for grapes, followed by soft fruit, spinach, savoy cabbage and kale, cucumber, peppers/chilli peppers, lemon and mushrooms. The insecticide acetamiprid accounted for the most limit exceedances (20%). There were also three MRL exceedances in products labelled organic (3.5%). © FreshPlaza Tomorrow, second part: A level playing field doesn't exist. But where is it lacking most? Beállítom The chair of the European Parliament's (EP) delegation that visited Hungary this week spoke on Wednesday about a “palpable change” in the country. Sophie Wilmès stressed that they had met with many people during their three-day visit—including representatives from the judiciary, civil society, and opposition parties, as well as members of the government and the president. According to her, the previous government was hostile, unwilling to cooperate, and under its rule, the situation continued to deteriorate. Among other things, this was seen in the fact that it governed through emergency decrees and fast-tracked legislation, there was pressure on the judiciary, the government’s narrative dominated the media, and independent organizations were forced to operate in a hostile environment. She noted that during their visit last year, they had also seen posters attacking European politicians. Since the government change, attacks against civic activists have ceased; the Constitutional Court can once again deliver rulings on tax-related matters; and its president is elected by the judges without political pressure. She also highlighted the establishment of the National Office for Asset Recovery and Protection (NVVH) and Hungary’s accession to the European Public Prosecutor’s Office. These steps have all had an impact: the Council of the European Union has terminated the rule-of-law conditionality procedure. She also added that limiting the term of parliamentary representatives to 12 years raised genuine concerns, noted shortcomings with regard to LGBTQ+ rights, and remarked that certain laws had been pushed through too hastily. The representatives also met with journalists associated with the previous government and inquired about the limits of the NVVH’s authority. Restoring the rule of law does not happen overnight, and they see that the will is certainly there, but it takes time. “The one million dollar question, of course remains the Article 7 procedure”, she said, adding that they won’t be drawing any conclusions on that now, because that’s not what they were authorized to do—they don’t represent the entire European Parliament—but they can provide information. The delegation from the European Parliament, consisting of eight MEPs, was visiting Hungary between October 26 to 28. According to an official statement from the European Parliament, the delegation reviewed the developments which have been implemented since the April 2026 election. What is the Article 7 procedure, and what does it have to do with this visit? During their visit, the representatives held consultations with senior government officials, parliamentary committees, and opposition parties. They also met with representatives of the Constitutional Court, the National Judicial Council, anti-corruption agencies, civil society organizations, and the press. The eight members of the European Parliament represent eight different parliamentary groups. The delegation was led by the liberal Sophie Wilmès. Joining her—as the sole Hungarian member—was András László from Fidesz. The far-left and far-right parliamentary groups each sent one member, while the Greens were represented by Tineke Strik. Strik is the rapporteur for the “Article 7” procedure, which the EP initiated against Hungary back in 2018 but which has made no progress since then. Under this procedure, certain rights arising from EU membership—such as a government’s voting rights—could be suspended if member state ministers determine that there has been a violation of the EU’s fundamental values, but they are nowhere near taking such a step. As Strik told Telex back in May, the fact-finding mission scheduled for this October will be “the perfect moment to consult with those involved” about whether they are satisfied with how things are working in practice. This could lead to our report including a recommendation for withdrawal.” A debate on the situation in Hungary has already been added to the agenda of the European Parliament’s plenary session scheduled for late November, with a vote expected on a resolution at the next session—a point Wilmès also alluded to on Wednesday. She did not want to go into details, but indicated that, as the initiator, the European Parliament would be taking the first step. At Wednesday’s press conference, Strik, like Wilmès, described the atmosphere as different from that during their previous visit—not only with regard to civil society groups but also with regard to the authorities, who were cooperative now. Like Wilmès, she saw progress, but she also noted that there are still areas in need of improvement—for example, as regards the refugee agency—where they would like to see a balanced system in place by the next election. A delegation and the parliamentary group (Patriots for Europe) the former Hungarian ruling parties belong to in the EP had proposed that the EP delegation also examine the circumstances under which Balázs Hankó, Miklós Seszták, and Balázs Bús are being held, but the delegation did not pay them a visit. Last year, the PfE did not delegate anyone for the same visit; according to Strik, at the time, the parliamentary group had decided to skip participation. Members of the Hungarian government at the time spoke of the visit being an attack against Hungary, claiming that “Péter “Brussels” and Kinga Kollár” had summoned them, even though similar delegations from the European Parliament regularly visit member states.
